utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-03-69-T, Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. While we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, I put on the record that the interviews of the present witness with the OTP have been -- the results of that have been made available to the Defence, and there has been some consultation yesterday, because the Prosecution would like to look at it as well, and after having consulted with the Defence, you have received the relevant interview results as well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We do understand now that time for cross-examination -- time --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. Our client cannot hear anything at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, then we have to take care of that. Mr. Stanisic, can you now hear me in a language you understand? I see you're nodding yes. I dealt with some practical problems over the weekend, that is the results of the interview being made available to the Defence and to the Prosecution as well, that the time estimate for cross-examination would be three to four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony is still binding, that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I was informed that you have been so kind to do the homework over the weekend and the first days after the weekend. Thank you for that. Mr. Groome asked for another 15 minutes for examination-in-chief. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would ask that the Court Officer please bring to our screens document 5294.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while we are waiting for that document to be brought to our screens, can I ask you were you provided a binder containing 14 documents, as well as a chart to record your assessment with respect to the authenticity of these documents over the last few days?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is the document that we can now see on our screens, is that the document in which you recorded your assessment with respect -- your assessment of the authenticity of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to the second page or the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, General, did you sign and date this document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that your signature at the bottom of this chart?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would ask the Court Officer to please bring to our screens document number 5295.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And while that is being done, General, were you also provided a binder of 40 documents to review, as well as a document to record your assessment of the authenticity of these documents, again over the last few days?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is the document that we now see on our screens an image of the document in which you recorded your comments with respect to the set of 40 documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can see a mistake under 8. I did not put my initials there, although I should have because the document is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So -- just so the record is clear, from what we can see, you did not put your initials in either column 5 or column 6. Where should your initials appear, which column, column 5 or column 6?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. In column 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And while that is being done, did you also sign and date at the end of the chart where you recorded your opinions as to these 40 documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I could ask that we move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that your signature that we can see at the bottom of the chart?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, just a few minutes ago, the Court Officer brought to my attention and to the attention of the Defence that there also in the binder that you returned appeared to be a handwritten letter in your handwriting. Is that correct, that you also provided a handwritten letter in the binder when you returned it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And my cursory -- the cursory explanation that has been provided to me is that it includes some other comments that you have made with respect to the documents that you were shown, and in an effort to be complete, you also made notes on this separate piece of paper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has an application with respect to these documents, but making such an application is likely to result in a detailed discussion of how they should be treated. In the interest of proceeding with the cross-examination and expediting General Milovanovic's evidence before the Chamber, the Prosecution simply asks at this time that the two documents be marked for identification and the detailed discussion of how they should be treated in this trial be deferred to a time later this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this about the comments and the notes or is it about the lists, the charts, that have been completed by Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My application relates to the two charts, document number 5294 and 5295.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you seek them to be marked for identification. Madam Registrar, the first chart dealing with 14 documents and the again --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 5294 becomes Exhibit P396, marked for identification. And 65 ter 5295 becomes Exhibit P397, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And both documents keep that status. They still are marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not knowing what is in the handwritten letter, I'm unable to express a view as to what I think should ultimately happen to the document, but perhaps it would be prudent to -- also at this time, to mark that for identification. And I'd ask that it be kept -- the original be kept in the custody of the Court Officer until the parties can discern what, if any, relevance it may have to this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has a copy already been given to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe copies have been given by the Court Officer to -- to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You received that, I see, that -- the Defence is nodding yes. Madam Registrar, a number -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. May I just, quickly, take some instructions from Mr. Stanisic? There's something about the B/C/S document which is of concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The B/C/S document being the handwritten edition to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Handwritten edition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, would it be possible to have a translation, the document read to us so that we can -- we English speakers can understand precisely what the handwritten note says at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got no idea how long it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: May I make a suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's about a page and a half. Perhaps during the first break I'll arrange to have someone here who can give a rough translation to all of us so that we can proceed with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then wait. Yes. The Chamber has received a hard copy. We're not seeking to understand it until you have had an opportunity. I see that it is a document which is handwritten, one and a half page long, and is -- the second page is dated the 25th of April, 2010, and from what I understand written here in The Hague, and it bears at the top "Manojlo Milanovic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry for mispronouncing your name. Then what to do with this document we'll wait for the parties to further address the Court after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution has no further questions of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we take it that -- Mr. Milovanovic, when you filled in those charts, you did it to the best of your abilities and in full accordance with what you think is the truth in this respect. That's, of course, a bit sensitive if you're talking about authenticity of documents, but you did it to the best of your abilities and -- is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is well understood, but I believe that I understood the task well, because the problem here is the problem of authenticity. And what is authenticity? In Serbian, "authentic" means the same, and since I was provided with the copies of the documents, I was supposed to use my experience and confirm that the copies are the same as their originals, and I did it in all 53 cases. In one case I could not establish that, that was in the penultimate document, and I put my initials under 6, in column 6, standing for non-authentic. I could not read the document, and I did not have the ERN numbers that were omitted while the document was being photocopied. That's why I identified that document as not being authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We find this explained under column 7 where you explain why you concluded or you were unable to conclude that it was authentic and therefore had to conclude that, as far as you could assess, that there could be no authenticity. Thank you for that answer. That's it, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. No questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Jordash, will you be the first one to cross-examine Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I represent Mr. Stanisic, so you understand who I am. I want to ask you, first of all, about something you said when you testified last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, please, could I have on e-court P392, which should be excerpt two from -- let me shortcut this. Could we go to the next page, please. Yes, this is what I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Last week you testified that you were confident that the Stanisic referred to in this exhibit was Mico Stanisic. Do you recall that. Evidence?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the name here, but I remember that I said that, because there was a bit of a dilemma which Stanisic was referred to, but here I can see in the text in the brackets Mico wrote the order, Bozovic to form a special at the public security centre in Doboj, and that's how I concluded that the Stanisic in question was Mico Stanisic, the then-minister in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this, it seems, was a note written about a meeting with political structures in Doboj. Do you see that heading?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saturday, Doboj, 6 -- 6th of February, 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you also testified that - I think this is -- let me try to paraphrase - at such meetings, the Stanisic who would be at the forefront of the -- those engaged in the meeting would be Mico Stanisic. If Jovica Stanisic was referred to, Jovica would be written down alongside Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I said so. However, I am increasingly more convinced that the person is Mico Stanisic, because we're talking about Doboj and the setting up of the Special Police Unit in Doboj. Jovica Stanisic never had anything to do with that. It was only the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska who could have anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you confirm that Mico Stanisic was the minister of the interior for Republika Srpska from March of 1992 until January of 1993? Sorry, let me start that again. From March 1992. That was the commencement of his post.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mico Stanisic was in that position in 1992 when the military was being set up, because I met with him on several occasions. How long he stayed in office, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you -- sorry. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was replaced by Ratko Adzic as minister of the interior, but I don't know when that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about what you've just said concerning the permission to set up the police -- Special Police Units in Doboj. It was only the minister of interior of Republika Srpska who could have anything to do with that. Could you clarify precisely what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I meant was this: When something is -- a unit is being set up with the Ministry of the Interior, that the person in charge of that would be the minister of the interior, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know that from your own experience or are you theorising about that generally?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only a hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you confirm Mico Stanisic was in that position at the beginning of 1992? The earlier part, if I can leave it like that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that. When the military or the Army of Republika Srpska was being set up, that was in May and June 1992, I met with Mico Stanisic on several occasions at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, and perhaps this is on the same subject but I do want to ask you about it, you said on -- last week that Jovica Stanisic would not be able to write an order to be located in Doboj in any case. Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you are quoting, what was said is that Jovica Stanisic would not have been able to write an order for the unit to be located in Doboj. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's almost a word-for-word quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the unit is -- who or what is located in Doboj doesn't appear in your quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The unit I'm referring to, Mr. Milovanovic, was the Red Berets, which we can see mentioned in Exhibit P392. And with reference to that, you said: "Jovica Stanisic would not have been able to write an order for the unit to be located in Doboj." What did you mean precisely by that, please? Why did you arrive at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are talking and if you're referring to the document that is now before us on the screen, I don't remember that I ever mentioned the Red Berets. I mentioned the centre of public security. And here General Mladic writes: "Mico wrote an order for Boskovic to set up a special unit with the public security centre in Doboj." I really don't remember ever having mentioned the term Red Berets in this particular context.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Bozovic being present in Doboj in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I learned that on Friday as I was looking at this piece of paper here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm correct -- it's correct, isn't it, that Mico Stanisic was the ultimate commander of the CJB security centre in Doboj in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mico Stanisic was the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could Exhibit -- Rule 65 ter 4359 be brought onto the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm going to give you a little time to read through this, Mr. Milovanovic, so you just have an understanding of what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that we cannot see the top line in B/C/S. I don't know whether the witness can, or does it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've just been told that apparently the B/C/S version does not match the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It now does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It now does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It didn't do a minute ago, but apparently it now does. That was also the reason why I wanted to see the top of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apparently this has been tendered as an exhibit already, P00383, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document please be scrolled up? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I do apologise. It looks as though there's some confusion. It's probably mine, but let me just try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we are back with the English we earlier had on our screen, but now apparently with the right B/C/S corresponding --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. This is the one that should have been there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not -- not easy for me to read. The letter's a bit too small. Could the document please be blown up a little? Could the document please be scrolled up. Could we please go down in the text. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did -- have you familiarised yourself with some of it, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with part of the text, but now I see page 2 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to page 3 then, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I haven't read through page 2 yet. Okay. Stay here. Could you please scroll down. Could you please scroll down some more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There seems to be no more. Possibly there's a page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There should be more than a page 3. Is this a document you have you've seen? Wasn't this a document you were asked to review previously?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen it in my life before today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just inquire then, is there only three pages in the B/C/S? Because it's a much longer document in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How could the witness know if he hasn't seen it before, Mr. Jordash? You can see in e-court that it's a six-page document in B/C/S. I mean, I can find it in a second. So, therefore, I take it -- and I can -- so why ask the witness who can look at one page on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was inquiring of the Registry, actually. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a six-page document, and it's signed -- or at least it's stamped at the bottom. I wouldn't say it's signed -- well, it's signed -- it has a stamp and a sign at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the remaining pages, please. I just want to make sure he's seen everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, I think this is a document you have seen and marked as authentic. Does it not look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I may have seen it these days during the proofing, but in operative use in the VRS I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm merely asking about whether you've seen it in the last few days so I can ask you questions about it without waiting for you to read it all again. Let me ask you some questions about it if I can since you've seen it before, marked it as authentic. Presumably you marked it as authentic in part because of the contents. Am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because of the content, because in one of those forms I wrote that I haven't read all the documents because there wasn't enough time, but I read practically all the headings and saw who wrote it and so on. We can see that this one was written by Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravko Tolimir was the assistant commander of the Main Staff of the VRS for intelligence- and security-related matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So this is a intelligence report dated the 28th of July, 1992, being sent to, as we can see, Department for OB Affairs of 1st Krajina, 2nd Krajina, Eastern Bosnia, Sarajevo, Romanija, and Hercegovina Corps, as well as SR BH RV and PVO, president of the SR BH Presidency, SR BH prime minister, SR BH Army Main Staff commander. Are you familiar with this type of intelligence report from 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in principle were the recipients the same as the recipients marked on this particular document? Is this where intelligence about paramilitaries went to from the intelligence and security sector of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the corps of the VRS are mentioned. It mentions also RV and PVO, but that's wrong. We didn't call it RV, which means "air force." And then it went to the president of the SR BH, the SR BH prime minister, and the commander of the Main Staff of the SR BH. It was not sent to me at the time. Speaking about such documents and intelligence, I can say that I never received any until mid 1993, because Tolimir thought we are sitting next to each other, but at meetings of the Main Staff I put forward my assessments of the situation in the combat theatre, but I didn't know this information. And then General Mladic got angry and started shouting at Tolimir, and then I started receiving such intelligence. That was around mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So just remind me, if you would. Your position from May of 1992 until mid-1993 was what? What was your assignment in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was Chief of Main Staff of the VRS, and, at the same time, according to the establishment, the deputy commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So from what you've said, from May of 1992, the establishment of the -- the date of the establishment of the VRS, until mid-1993, you were not receiving intelligence about the operations of paramilitary groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can't say that I didn't receive information. I did receive information from Tolimir and the chief of the intelligence administration, Colonel Salapura, but only in direct contact, without any written communication. Simply, the chief of the intelligence administration Salapura, if he had any news about the enemy, he would come to see me and brief me orally. Tolimir did the same if he had anything that was security related. I remember some things from this particular document. I remember this Zuco guy --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. -- sorry to interrupt, Mr. Milovanovic. I'm going to ask you about the document in a minute. I just want to ask you about the information you were receiving. Mladic, in the middle of 1993, was perturbed, let me put it that way, that his Chief of Staff was not receiving proper information about the activities of paramilitaries in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as far as you were aware during this period, that intelligence was going only to the named people in this report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that can be seen at the bottom of this page. This is the only correct thing compared to what I read over the weekend, I mean, the 54 documents. I said and can confirm now that both in peacetime and in war time there is the obligation for intelligence and security services of friendly countries in a region to co-operate, and General Tolimir was duty-bound to inform the commanders of all subordinate units. Furthermore, to inform the intelligence administration of the General Staff of the VJ, as a neighbouring armed force. Furthermore, the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of the Krajina, which I -- which is not indicated here or I may have skipped it. And if he considers it necessary to inform the Commander-In-Chief of something and the commander of the Main Staff of his own army, he had to do so. All the other names that -- and I said that in relation to the document put forward by the Prosecutor, he would also pass on to the General Staffs of the armies of neighbouring countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me try to understand that. Are you suggesting this intelligence in 1992 went to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should have been passed on to them, but I can see here that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So is it your understanding that it was being sent to the VJ in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only say it should have been sent to them. Why this does -- why this isn't indicated on the document among the addressees, I don't know, but not even the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of the Krajina is mentioned here as one of the recipients, and it should have gone there. All the documents that I've seen in these few days, these two are mentioned as recipients, and that's what I said in my additional comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The documents, we'll come to some of them later, but the documents that you have looked at where, for example, Jovica Stanisic is copied as a member -- as the chief of the state security of Serbia, were from 1993 in the main. Could I suggest that 1992 intelligence such as this was not being sent to the Republic of Serbia? If it had been, I would suggest the names would have been on this document.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I repeat that I don't know whether documents in 1992 were sent to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I cannot tell from this document. And the documents that are reviewed these days mostly relate to 1993 and 1994, and there I saw that it was indicated in each document that they were sent there. Mr. President, since Defence counsel insists that I explain to him something that I have already explained in my letter, I suggest that I read out the letter which the interpreters can interpret. It is not long. It's handwritten, one and a half page, so typed it would be less than one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we left if in the hands of the parties until now what to do with the document, but if you say that an answer to a question which was put to you by Mr. Jordash is found in this letter, under those circumstances I would suggest that we follow this offer, and we invite you then to read it. But it's common experience that, when reading, speed of speech goes up. So if you would really keep the pace low. Do you have the letter in front you, or would you need to be provided with a copy? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just received it. Can I start reading?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I reviewed in detail all information enclosed which Colonel Zdravko Tolimir or his deputies Beara and Salapura, that is, Ljubisa Beara and Petar Salapura, sent to various addresses in parts of the former SFRY. I feel duty-bound to explain the following: "1. It is common practice for friendly countries in peacetime and war time to exchange intelligence. That is done at the level of the intelligence services of General Staffs or Main Staffs respectively. "As far as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is concerned, Tolimir is duty-bound to submit information only to the intelligence administration of the General Staff of the army of the SRJ and nobody else in Yugoslavia, and the chief of that administration decides who in his country he will acquaint with that information." Okay. "And the chief of the intelligence administration of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia decides who in his country he will acquaint with this information, whether it should be the Chief of General Staff, the state head, this or that government minister, or anybody else. It follows that there is no need to list other institutions in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, least of all the persons at -- who are heads of those institutions, including Jovica Stanisic or anybody else. "Secondly, it follows from this information that Tolimir, Beara, and Salapura regularly mentioned the name of Jovica Stanisic, General Djordje Djukic, chief of the nationality security of Republika Srpska Dragan Kijac, Colonel Spiro Pereula. Spiro Pereula is Tolimir's man installed in the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. And the names of Zoran Sokolovic, minister of the interior of Serbia, and one Blagojevic, the federal minister of the interior of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as well as my name are mentioned. "If you take a closer look, you will see that those are the names of people who hold higher ranks or higher positions than Tolimir. So this was meant to prove that he is in direct communication with 'important' persons from the region. Never was the name of anybody from the Republic of Serb Krajina mentioned (they are not important) or from commands subordinate to ours to who information was sent. "Thirdly, because of all this, I wanted to point it out to you that in the about 160 pages of Tolimir's intelligence that is enclosed, their contents either incriminates or exculpates Mr. Jovica Stanisic. The administration of the Tribunal was only unnecessarily burdened with a large quantity of paper. "The Hague, 24 April 2010, Manojlo Milovanovic."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 25 April 2010, that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if other people heard it, but I thought that I heard at page 20, line 21, that the word "either" was, in fact, "neither." It seems to contextually make more sense, but maybe Mr. Jordash could clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, just to clarify something that was said by you and may have been recorded mistakenly, could you just repeat the line which starts off with "Thirdly, because of all this ..."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Thirdly, because of all this, I wanted to point out to you that the enclosed pages of Tolimir's intelligence, about 160 pages of it, do not either incriminate or exculpate Mr. Jovica Stanisic. The administration of the Tribunal was only unnecessarily burdened with a large quantity of paper."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This, I think, clarifies the issue. I see also the negations and in the original text we see nay, nay, and the context is also better understandable, that he says it neither does, nor, and therefore it was an unnecessary burden. That last part is, by the way, your opinion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just try to make sure I understand what you're saying in this note. Are you suggesting that the document we've been looking at from Tolimir, which doesn't contain the name of officials from the Republic of Serbia, would not ordinarily have been expected to contain the name of officials from Serbia because that wasn't the way intelligence was passed to them?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not surprised. That's my question, which was a bit long. Are you -- are you suggesting that it was normal protocol for intelligence to be sent to those named in this document; thereafter, the chief of administration would make a decision as to what was passed on to other republics?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only was it customary, but it was prescribed. Co-operation with partnership countries should have been established at the level of the services of the same ranks. Since I'm talking about the Military Intelligence Service of Republika Srpska, that service had to exchange information with military service of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or, rather, with the General Staff of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And now there were other institutions that co-operated with each other, for example, State Security Services.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Witness, may I just stop you there. Is it -- is this correct: You actually cannot testify to what intelligence was or was not being passed to the Republic of Serbia in 1992? You can talk about what was customary, but you actually do not know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging from the 54 reports that I've read these days, it is clear that the intelligence service of Republika Srpska overstepped its authorities. And let me be more precise. It overstepped the authorities that were prescribed. Instead of just communicating with the intelligence service of the General Staff of Yugoslavia, it communicated with all the services in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Not in Serbia but in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, for which Tolimir deemed it necessary that they should communicate with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1992. Did you see any reports in -- dated 1992 with intelligence concerning paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the general wasn't given any reports from 1992, so I think it's a somewhat misleading question to say reports from 1992 that had certain information in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, that was the point I was trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You didn't look at any reports from 1992, and my question was focused on 1992. You cannot testify to what intelligence was being passed to the Republic of Serbia in 1992. Is that a fair proposition?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are partially right. I have told you that in 1992 I did not receive any intelligence. I only started receiving intelligence report in mid-1993. So I was not in a position to know who Tolimir sent it to. Second of all, I said, and I believe that made you draw an erroneous conclusion, I said that I do know certain things. I spoke about that on Friday. I do know certain things about that person Zuco from Zvornik, and I also know something but not from this intelligence but from other sources, from the reports submitted to me by subordinated units about the disappearance or the theft according to the information that I had at the time of anything between 2 and 11 tons of silver from Sase mine. As soon as I received that information, I reported to President Karadzic who told me he -- he told me then that that was not within the purview of the army, that that was not our business.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why were you, the Chief of Staff, not receiving written reports until mid-1993 about what must have been one of the critical military issues in Bosnia-Herzegovina during 1992 and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive it because that was not prescribed at the time. It was the commander of the Main Staff who received such reports. And then at his own discretion he was supposed to brief his assistants, the assistants that he himself selected. However, this was done by General Mladic because although we had -- or we shared an office during the war, we never stayed in the same office at the same time. When he was there, I was on the line and vice versa. And that's when he decided that I should collect information about the enemy through Colonel Salapura and through the commands of subordinate units. Or according to him, and I quote: "I don't want my deputy to collect intelligence in trenches."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go back to the document quickly. The first paragraph of -- states: "Paramilitary formations and groups are an important feature of the war in the former Yugoslavia. The paramilitary formations on SR BH territory have special identifying names such as Arkan's men, Seselj's men, Captain Dragan's commandos, Captain Oliver's commandos, Jovic's men, White Eagles, Wolves, Smoked Ribs, and the like." Now, in July 1992 were you aware of these groups, you as the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Friday I spoke about the way the General Staff treated paramilitaries. I spoke about Arkan's men. They disappeared in May 1992 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, I want to try to get finished as quickly as possible, so if you could try to address my questions directly. Were you aware of these groups in May -- sorry, in July of 1992? Were you aware of them on BiH territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it all depended. I was aware of Arkan's men, but they were no longer in the territory. I heard of Seselj's men, but I never saw them, nor did anybody tell me that they had come in conflict with Seselj's men. Whatever arrived from the territory of Serbia, the territory of Republika Srpska, whoever arrived, they tended to introduce themselves as Seselj -- Seselj's men. About Captain Dragan, I told you on Friday what happened to them. As for commandos headed by Captain Oliver, I never heard of them before. As for Carli's men, I don't think that they were an organised paramilitary formation. Carli's men were those people who opened fire from mounted mortars. Carli was the name that we gave to those weapons. As for Jovic's men, they did not exist in the territory of Republika Srpska. There were some attempts on the part of Jovic to build them into the armed formations of Republika Srpska, but we disallowed that. White Eagles, I heard of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of two types of Wolves, Wolves from Vucjak headed by lieutenant Milankovic, they were incorporated in the 1st Corps and they came under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska. And then there were the Drina Wolves, and that was a special unit on the strength of the Drina Corps. As for Smoked Ribs, I only learned about them from Tolimir's intelligence. During the war, I was never aware of them. I never heard of them during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Could I turn, please, to page 5 of the English version. I want to just read you something. In -- and it says this at paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we turn to that in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "In the area of the Serbian municipality of Skelani, a camp of so-called Red Berets was established headed by Nikola Pupovac, one of Captain Dragan's pupils." Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that between the 16th and the 21st of January. On the 16th, the exodus of the Serbian population started in the area around Skelani. I personally issued an order for two battalions to arrive from the 1st Krajina Corps, and that was done within the three or four days. On the 21st, I went to Skelani to see what had been done by those two battalions. The population started returning by then. And then I heard that in the Skelani sector - and I don't know in which village exactly - a group of six -- 26 Serbs who had come from across the Drina from Serbia had been discovered and they introduced themselves in different ways, but they mostly spoke about themselves as Seselj's Chetniks. I reported back to the commander on the same evening, and he ordered Tolimir -- or, rather, Beara, the head of security, to make that group disappear. And that's all I can tell you. I found it very strange when I read about that in one of the reports that I perused recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So are you making a connection between Captain Dragan's pupil Nikola Pupovac and the Red Berets and Seselj's men? I just want to understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Among people, Seselj's men was a general term for everybody who came to Republika Srpska from somewhere else. They referred to themselves either to disguise their identity or for some other reasons. They said that they belonged to Seselj and they were Seselj's Chetniks. Everybody but Arkan's men. All those groups that turned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the intelligence that -- is this correct: The intelligence that you received in 1992 about Dragan's men, was that limited then to -- let me put it differently. Did you know where they were from other than Serbia? Was there any intelligence concerning why they had come?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring specifically to Captain Dragan's men?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the report. There's no suggestion that there was any intelligence as to where they came from. Was that the state of your knowledge in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew, when Captain Dragan appeared in Divic near Zvornik, that a few men came with him from Knin, from the Republic of Serbian Krajina. He had been their commander over there. And we also knew that he was joined by several men from Republika Srpska. And we also knew that most of the men who were with him were from Serbia. However, I told you that that group obeyed me and left the Drina area sometime in mid-June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So they were known at that time by no other name than Captain Dragan's men except that they sometimes referred to themselves as Seselj's men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we are talking about Captain Dragan's men, I did not hear anybody referring to them as Seselj's men. They themselves did not call themselves that. I have told you that whenever people from somewhere else appeared, the local population would be told that they were Seselj's men, and that's the kind of intelligence we received from the ground. We would always hear about such men appearing as Seselj's men, and it really rarely proved to be true, if ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Captain Dragan's men are described in paragraph one as Captain Dragan's commandos. Is that how you as the Chief of Staff knew them in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would really be embarrassed to use the name that I called them before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why, is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. I note the time, Your Honour. Could I ask one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know what you're going to say, but since you offered it, could you say what name you referred to them as?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally called them renegade, thieving bastards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And other people called them Captain Dragan's commandos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this text you can see the term "Captain Dragan's commandos." Tolimir is the author of the text, so you can draw your own conclusion as to how the author or Tolimir called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If I could just finish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I know Tolimir referred to him as that. We know what you referred to them as. Were they known generally amongst the VRS, from your knowledge and experience of personnel within the VRS, as Captain Dragan's commandos? That's what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they were referred to, but I repeat for the umpteenth time, from the 23rd of June when the mobilisation of the Army of Republika Srpska finished, they did not have any of the aforementioned groups under its command. In other words, the Army of Republika Srpska did not contain any paramilitary formations. Some continued bearing their names, as, for example, Wolves, but they were on the strength of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I apply to tender that document as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection. In fact, I think we have tendered it and it was marked for identification based on opposition from counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. Can I withdraw the opposition that I expressed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Implicitly you have done so already, Mr. Jordash. And it had received a number already. It was P383, MFI'd, and is now admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just ask you quickly -- let me just ask you quickly, Mr. Milovanovic, about Arkan and two particular events. Did Arkan have a relationship with Rajko Dukic in or about 1994?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about 1994, but in or about June 1992 I know that he had contact with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Rajko Dukic was practically like Karadzic's deputy, is that right, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the name is not Djukic, it is Dukic. He was the director of the Boksit mine in Milici, and he was the president of the Executive Committee of the SDS, and that would be the rank equal to the deputy president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the municipality was -- was this the municipality of Milici?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. You mean does it refer to Dukic at Milici or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me strike that question and let me ask you this: Did Dukic employ Arkan? Did he engage him?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the date, but it must have been in June 1992 when Dukic came to the Main Staff and he spoke to General Mladic. He suggested to him that the Main Staff allow Dukic to employ 120 Arkan's Tigers to guard the mine. General Mladic took the newspapers and replied, Tell that story to my chief, because he likes rubbish. And Dukic started talking that he needed 120 men, that he would pay -- or, rather, the management of the mine for guarding the mine. And I said to him, Sir, we went to great ends in May and June to get rid of paramilitaries, especially of Arkan, and said that was out of the question. And he started enumerating to me where we should deploy units, that is, a company round the mine to enable that mine to function properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. -- sorry to interrupt. Was Arkan employed on behalf of Dukic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Dukic's request sanctioned by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Arkan subsequently employed by Dukic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I must say that after that conversation with Dukic, who demanded about 26 companies of the VRS, I said to him, That's two and a half brigades. We don't have as many soldiers. He said to me, General, as you are from the Krajina, bring some people from the Krajina. I refused that. Actually, Mladic threw him out of the office. In the evening, I informed the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic, of that conversation with Dukic, and Karadzic said to me, Disband them or scatter them if they should turn up again. But they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Karadzic order Arkan to come on his behalf in September of 1995 to BiH?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is still a mystery to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What is a mystery to you? You know, don't you, that Arkan was engaged by Karadzic to take over Kljucic in September of 1995? You've dealt with this in a previous interview; we can turn to it if you want. Or you can cast your mind back and see if you remember to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I supposed to remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, do you recall Arkan being engaged by Karadzic to take over Kljucic on the 16th of September, 1995? Let me remind you a bit further. You and Mladic subsequently banished Arkan, having disagreed with Karadzic's decision.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I used the word "mystery," that's a lone word in the Serbian language and means something that I don't know, something unknown to me. That is why I'm saying that it is still a mystery to me how Arkan turned up in the Republika Srpska. What you call Kljucic is the town of Kljuc which the VRS lost on that 16th of September, and I don't know that Arkan asked for permission to take Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask one more. And if you can't remember, we can turn to the interview. Karadzic brought Arkan to Kljuc, and you and Mladic made an agreement that Arkan should be banished, notwithstanding Karadzic's authorisation. Try and assist us if you can.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to assist you. Arkan appeared without the knowledge of the VRS, that is, without the knowledge of the Main Staff. He appeared at the theatre of war in the RS in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I'm short of time. Did Karadzic -- do you remember Karadzic having a part to play in this or not? If you don't remember, we'll turn to the interview. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic had a role to play, but I don't know exactly what. I don't know if Karadzic ordered Arkan to come or whether he had invited him to come to the RS. Karadzic always denied that. Whereas Arkan, at a meeting, in Karadzic's presence said to me that he had come, following the orders of President Karadzic. And he even used the phrase "our supreme commander" to refer to him. In Karadzic's presence, I demanded Arkan to produce that order, because we in the Main Staff doubted the existence of that order. We had never seen it. He said he had left the order in the Bosna Hotel. I told him to go there and get it, but later he changed his mind, and my conclusion was that there was no such order. I asked Karadzic in the presence of Arkan, Mr. Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, General Talic, and General Kelecevic, I said, Mr. President, did you ask or order Arkan to come? And Karadzic did not reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Karadzic didn't reply and he didn't deny that he had; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have please --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on e-court P386, MFI'd. And could we -- this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you see the front page there, Mr. Milovanovic? Can you confirm that you've had the opportunity, I think, during the preparation sessions, to look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the opportunity, and I looked at it. But I didn't have time to read it, nor did I want to because I was one of the authors of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well let me take you to page 49. I just want to ask you some very quick questions and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Forty-nine we should start with and the quoting of ... the same page for the B/C/S, I think. No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Maybe we can shortcut it in this way: Could I read you a paragraph and see if you recognise the paragraph, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For Your Honours, it's page 49 of the English version, and it's the first full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "The unfavourable political and security situation immediately before the war, and the break-up of the intelligence and security system, which resulted from the stratification along ethnic lines of, especially, the commanding staff in the intelligence and security organs, had a rather adverse effect on the combat morale of the core fighting units from which the army of RS was formed." Do you recall that paragraph in this combat readiness report reporting on 1992, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see that paragraph in front of me, and it's unrealistic to expect me to remember a paragraph after 18 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The page in B/C/S seems to be in e-court page 44 out of 142, which starts with 2.2, manifestations of morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I should have found the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if -- so, therefore, it -- most likely it's even 43, which is the last portion before paragraph 2.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you see the paragraph? If you could read it to yourself, Mr. Milovanovic, beginning with "The unfavourable political and security situation ..."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see page 43, whereas the President of the Trial Chamber mentioned page 44. I cannot see what you're asking me on page 43. Now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please scroll down. I have read the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you agree that the intelligence and security system in 1992 of the VRS was way below competent, which affected, as the paragraph suggests, the combat morale of the core fighting unit?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the authors of this text is the section of morale, legal, and religious affairs of the Main Staff. This is not an assessment of the intelligence and security service of the VRS, but this is, rather, an assessment of the morale, the undeveloped or poor system that existed at the beginning of the war, that is, in May, June, et cetera. When the VRS was established, was being established, the intelligence and the security service was being established parallelly. And General Gvero, who was in charge of these issues, mentions one of the reasons why combat morale was below the required level when the VRS was only being incepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Could we turn, please, to 83 in the English version, which is 74 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you -- is this section familiar to you, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a chapter I know. One of the authors of this chapter is probably Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you agree with the assessment at the bottom of -- well, the English version, bottom of 83, the paragraph I'm interested in reads: "Due to financial constraints and the inability to provide any safety guarantees whatsoever to non-Serb operational sources in our territory, we did not manage to preserve the existing or recruit new high-quality sources in enemy territory. We therefore focused on sources motivated by patriotism (mostly Serbs and friends) who, being known as such in a hostile environment, had no access to significant intelligence data." Do you agree with that? Could you elaborate on it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with this assessment, because in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was above all an inter-ethnic war, and then it was also a civil war and a religious war, et cetera. So we were, at least in the beginning, unable to develop sources on the enemy side. So we couldn't really develop secret agents or whatever the technical term is. You mentioned the term "Serbia," but this isn't about Serbia. It is about Serbs and their friends. I fully agree with the contents of this paragraph, because these are always the ailnesses when the -- when intelligence services are first developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 85 of the English version, please, which is page 76 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I'm interested in the paragraph which is one, two, three, four, five, six paragraphs down on page 85 of the English version and starts with: "Co-operation and exchange of data with related services in the territory of RS is generally satisfactory, as well as with the Main Staff of the SVRSK. Of late, co-operation has been -- also been intensified with the intelligence and security organs of the Army of Yugoslavia, while with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia it is still at an unsatisfactory level." Do you see that, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this an accurate assessment of the intelligence sharing with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot either confirm or deny because I wasn't familiar with the details of who we were co-operating with or not co-operating, because, after all, this wasn't anything that I had to take care of in the Main Staff. This wasn't my business.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this as an exhibit, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection. If the Chamber will recall, this is one of the documents that we tendered last week, and the Chamber took the view that since it was of such a large size that we should meet and discuss with Defence whether we could agree on certain excerpts. So I was prepared to do that. But on principle, I have no objection to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'd be content to, if Your Honours prefer, just to have the pages I referred to in. I will undoubtedly over the next few months refer to it some more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it -- it should also include -- in the beginning we see that there is a kind of an index or at least -- so that we know what the whole of the document is about and then if [indiscernible]. Now, Mr. Groome, could you assist me. Had we already assigned an MFI number to it, or was it just open?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe there is a MFI number to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's P386 [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P386 will then keep the status of MFI, and the parties are invited to -- to reduce the size of what should be admitted from this document, and then the Chamber is aware that that could be enlarged at later stages of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I have P00258 on e-court, please. It should be a map which is number 35 in the book provided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm moving, as that comes onto the screen, Mr. Milovanovic, to your comments and your meeting with Mr. Stanisic on the 23rd of January, 1993 at Tara that you referred to last week. And last week you expressed surprise or certainly in the unit transcript video you referred to Mr. Stanisic's knowledge as somewhat surprising. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I said that I was full of admiration for the man's good knowledge of Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm trying to have them --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's coming. 258, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to deal with this meeting in a wider context, and the context I want to deal with it in is the attacks by Naser Oric. Is -- the meeting at Tara was about how to defend the Serbian border from Naser Oric's men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. The meeting was held about the principal topic of the ways and means of assisting the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which they had been attacked by the Croats who had violated the Vance-Owen Plan. Martic demanded assistance from me, but I was unable to provide it. He wanted air force support. And I forwarded the request to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who was duty-bound to do it because they were a guarantor of the Vance-Owen Plan, but Karadzic and Mladic, who were in London, I believe, answered -- or, rather, agreed that I should have a meeting with General Panic from the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina to find a way to help them. We were supposed to meet on the 23rd of January at Tara, but on the same day the hydro power plant of Visegrad was attacked, which was a joint hydro power plant. That became more of a problem for me than the Republic of Serbian Krajina. While I was waiting for General Panic with my team, I learned that in a village around Visegrad, I believe it's Mokronozi, but I'm not sure, from the morning until the afternoon hours, that is, or about 2.00, some 2- or 300 Serb civilians had been killed. So that was the situation. I was explaining that to Panic on the map, but we were unable to reach any agreement without Panic, but he was -- he couldn't make any decisions without his supreme commander, Dobrica Cosic, who was abroad. While I was explaining the situation in Eastern Bosnia to Panic, Jovica Stanisic assisted me, who knew that area very well it turned out. Jovica and I didn't even discuss amongst ourselves. I, at most, confirmed some things that Jovica said, and I merely -- I was merely saying that he knew about those things better than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Naser Oric's men attack Serbian -- Bosnian Serb territory in May of 1992? Could you explain what happened?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser Oric's attacks against Serbian villages and hamlets around Srebrenica started before the armed conflicts officially started between Muslims and Serbs. He organised something that the Muslims called Patriotic League or the Red Berets that preceded the official establishment of the BiH Army. I'm not sure of the exact date, although these days I have been reading a book called "Serbian Slaughter Execution Sites." In any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, I think I may have misspoken and said May of 1993, but I meant to say May of 1992. Oric's men went on the rampage in early 1992 and attacked 56 villages in the Drina region around Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you are quoting me and the things that I said yesterday. I said 156 villages and hamlets. I know that 91 villages and hamlets were completely destroyed in the process, and I know that in that part of the Drina area there were some 9.000 Serbs. Up to February 1993, from March 1992 to February 1993, a total of 3.200 Serbs were killed in the area. The rest were expelled. As a result of that, in central Drina region between Zvornik and Zepa only 9 per cent of the Serbs remained. The villages were empty, plundered, destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you see the map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, although it is not very legible. The letters are very small. I can see Visegrad, however. I can see Srebrenica clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, is it possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milovanovic be given a pen to mark on the map where these attacks were taking place along the border.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait for a second, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a little so Mr. Milovanovic can see it properly and then can mark on the map where these attacks took place, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, if you could give instructions as to what area we need which would allow you to mark the attacks. Is this the right portion or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from this position -- or, rather, at this moment I cannot start listing the villages for you. I could if somebody first gave me their names. I couldn't say yes or no. It really isn't easy to start listing all the 156 villages and hamlets. I really wouldn't know where to start. In any case, I'm talking about the villages around Srebrenica, south of Srebrenica. For example, Podravno is something that rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you if could indicate the area, if it is one area. Then you could just put a circle around that area once a pen has been given to you. Is that possible on this map, or is the area too small or too large?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We will not get a larger number of villages if the map is blown up. Let's start with Srebrenica, for example, and then south of Srebrenica on the very border is Podravno, or Podravanje as we used to call it. That's one of the villages that got destroyed. And then if we go northward towards Srebrenica, there is the village of Zeleni Jadar. And then, to the west, Bucje, Dile, Rupovo Brdo, Suceska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see -- Mr. Jordash, may I take it that you would be happy to have at least some of these villages and not all 156.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I see several of the villages which Mr. Milovanovic is mentioning on that map. So could we invite you that whenever you see a village on the map that you encircle it so that we can see it as well. I think you started with Podravno.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would perhaps read the names when you are ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's start all over again. Podravno, Bucje, Suceska, Rupovo Brdo, Dile, Zeleni Jadar, Osmace, Brezani, Poznanovici, Mocevici, Obadi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, thank you. Could I maybe shortcut things and ask you to confirm this: The attacks took place along the border from Zvornik to Visegrad. Zvornik in the north, which we cannot see on the map quite, just above --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps we can move the map down a little so we can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can't move and zoom in or out any more once --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree with that, Mr. Milovanovic, that the attacks took place along the border from approximately Zvornik down to Visegrad which is south of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From Zvornik down to a hill called Zlovrh or it's part of Susica Mountain. It is down to there that the criminals of Naser Oric plundered. They were not an organised army. They were just armed locals. They attacked Serb villages from Muslim villages. They destroyed it and torched it. South of Zlovrh in the direction of Visegrad, there were others who operated. I don't know what their formations were called, but, in any case, they were Muslims from the territory of Zepa and some other towns down there whose names I can't remember. In any case, they were a different group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Naser Oric have any foreign Muslims in his midst at that time? Was there any Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I never received intelligence in 1992 about the existence of any Mujahedin. Subsequently I learned that they appeared in the second half of 1993. I saw a footage depicting a decapitated man called Blagojevic with a Mujahedin. I don't know how many there were in this part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come to that later. But, nonetheless, Serb civilians were being brutalised by thousands of Oric's men at that time along this border that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I am trying hard to locate the village of Kravice. I can't see it. In the course of a single day, 61 persons were killed there, predominantly civilians, predominantly women and elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Naser Oric also attack Skelani in early January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 16th to the 21st of January, 1993, I believe that those men belonged to Naser. I've already spoken about those incidents. Not only do I think, I am actually sure that they were Naser's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we please have another copy of this map on the screen so we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then this one should first be saved and assigned a number, then, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Actually, sorry, Your Honour, I can see Skelani there on the map. That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Skelani is close, by Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Skelani, Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll apply to tender in a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Skelani is a border town with a bridge over to Banja Basta in Serbian territory -- Serbian territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skelani is in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and across the Drina is Bajina Basta, immediately across the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And following that attack, there were incursions into Bajina Basta; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any incursions by people, but I know that Bajina Basta was plundered from the left bank of the Drina because people were fleeing across the only bridge between Skelani and Bajina Basta. And there were shots fired after the population fleeing into Serbia, and I believe some of the shells or infantry ammunition hit buildings in Bajina Basta as well. And I know that there were protests from Serbia and that was -- that it was reported on the news that Bajina Basta had come under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this was a significant event because it was perhaps one of the first times that the border had been violated by Naser Oric's troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was the first instance, but I know that it was not an only one. Mali Zvornik also came under mortar fire from the left bank of the Drina onto the right bank of the Drina, but I don't know when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
