utterances.text: Could I have, please, on the -- could I tender this map as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked -- map marked by the witness, Madam Registrar, would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D39, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D39 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We admitted into evidence what you wanted us to admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've -- you mentioned the Vance-Owen Plan a moment ago. Was there a provision within that plan for Yugoslavia to assist the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not the Vance-Owen Plan. The Vance-Owen Plan was applicable to Bosnia. We have to talk about the Vance Plan, the one that was issued in May and June 1992, according to which fighting was stopped in the Republic of Croatia. UNPA or pink zones were established for the Serbs, and they were placed under the protection of -- of the United Nations. Croats were not allowed to attack those pink zones, and Serbs in the pink zones were not allowed to launched attacks on Croats. The arms of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was placed under the key and lock, and a copy of that key was held by the United Nations or UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there a provision within that Vance Plan for Yugoslavia to assist the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A guarantor of the Vance Plan for the Republic of Serbian Krajina was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I believe that it was provided for. If the Croats attacked one of those UNPROFOR protected areas, they could use arms to put the situation right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I have, please, on the screen V000-2061, but it's the transcript I'm looking for, not the video. 1561, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want, if you would, Mr. Milovanovic, to read through this transcript and see if you recognise the event and you recognise hearing this item on the TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I get the impression that we are not on the same page in English and B/C/S, or are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't think we are, because the timings are different at the top left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there's music in the B/C/S, whereas there seems to be no music in the English. Try to find the right --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think if we move past the music to the line "This morning the delegation ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but now in B/C/S, because if you -- let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, are you reading this? If you are, then just indicate when you want the transcript to move.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading. Yes, I'm reading. I'm reading. You can move the text now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think the problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever the witness is reading, it seems that we do not have the corresponding portions of English and B/C/S on our screen. Did you want to start at 1:1:48? Is that where you wanted to start, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's try to find that in B/C/S as well. Otherwise, the witness reads for nothing. Let's see where we are. What about page 35 in B/C/S, Mr. Jordash? Would that be a good suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could read for 6 pages, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading. Can you move the text now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the English one, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the English one. Could we go to page 2 of the English one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested, Mr. Milovanovic, at timings 1:41:04, where it -- and I'll read it: "The Serbian Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic and Interior Minister Zoran Sokolovic visited Bajina Basta today holding talks on the security situation in this border belt area. On the north Dalmatian battle-field of the offensive, the Croatian armed forces against Krajina positions continues. In Budapest, the commander of NATO forces in positions in Europe, John Shaljkashvilj told journalists that the crisis in Yugoslavia can only be solved politically and not militarily."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have none of that on the screen, whatever you have just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm going to shortcut this. I do apologise. Something has gone wrong with our administration. Let me ask you this: Were you aware that there were talks and a visit by Sainovic and Sokolovic to the Bajina Basta region as a result of the fragile security of the border following Naser Oric's attacks?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember if I knew of it at the time. However, a few days ago during the proofing session or maybe here in the courtroom, I watched a documentary depicting Sainovic's and Sokolovic's stay in Bajina Basta. They inspected a unit there, and that was a police unit. Now I remember; that was during my proofing session with the Prosecutor. And among all those people I saw military policemen with a white belt. Somebody asked me about that policeman, how come that he was there. I suppose that he was from the Uzice Corps providing security for somebody or something. So I can't say that I am not aware of that event, but I really can't tell you whether I remembered -- remember it from the period of a war, when it actually happened. And it happened sometime after the 21st of January, once the Skelani crisis, if I may call it so, was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from your experience, if Sokolovic, as the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia, had visited Bajina Basta to deal with the security on the border, would you be surprised or would it be perfectly normal for the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia to be concerned with incursions into the border?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that he was worried, but how come that only the minister of the interior came and not the minister of defence? I don't know what the situation is like in Serbia today, but it seems to me that at that time the border was controlled by the police of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia rather than the army. A few days ago we spoke about who manned the border crossing, that there were police and customs. So it is normal that the minister of the interior came there, because he's in charge of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the same question in terms of the state security of Serbia. Would it surprise you in such a situation that the state security of Serbia would be interested in incursions into the border?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security of Serbia is responsible for the entire territory of Serbia, for the safety of the citizens respective of where they are, along the border or further inland.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Milovanovic, that as a consequence of the attacks by Oric a decision was made by the Serbian leadership to mount Operation Drina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose operation that was, and what do you -- and what do you mean by Serbian leadership? The leadership of the Republic of Serbia or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I -- that's what I meant. Let me simplify the question. Had you -- have you heard of Operation Drina arising from attacks by Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't heard of the Drina operation, but I heard of the Podrinje '93 operation, which we prepared. Then there was Pesnica operation, which translates as "fist." Then there is a Krivaja operation, but I can't recall Drina operation. We had an Operational Group that was called Drina, which was in the area of Kalinovik, Cajnice, Visegrad. I know that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had an Operational Group called Drina, but it was on the other side. They were part of the Uzice Corps. As far as I know, the commander of that Operational Group was General Sipcic, but that Operational Group called Drina did not -- wasn't active on the left bank but on the right bank of the Drina. That was a precautionary measure to prevent the repetition of these attacks from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. You spoke last week about being surprised about Jovica Stanisic's knowledge of Klotijevac, which is close to Skelani. Could you explain why you were surprised, given what was happening along that border and the attacks on that border by Naser Oric? What was the basis for your amazement, using your words?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that. I was amazed because I had never heard of that village until that time. And upon returning to the Main Staff, I had great difficulty finding it on the map, but I did eventually. So a person who wasn't from Bosnia-Herzegovina and knew the geography of Bosnia-Herzegovina to such minute details, it was hardly surprising that I was amazed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that consequently as a result of the attacks by Oric the public security of the Republic of Serbia began to be trained at Tara, trained to protect the border more efficiently? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of training in Tara at that time of men who were subsequently engaged in protecting the border?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave that, then, for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just take instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I do not know what your instructions are at this moment, but we're close to the time we would have a break. And I have to deal with a few procedural matters. So to the extent that fits into your instructions, that -- I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That fits. That's a natural break, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then since the first part should be dealt with in private session -- Mr. Milovanovic, we'll have a break and we have to deal with some practical matters that are unrelated to you, so I would allow you already to follow the usher and leave the courtroom. We'll resume in approximately half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are no requests. The Prosecution does not intend to request them. But given some of the unusual circumstances, we wanted to proceed in case the Chamber felt differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I put on the record that, in relation to Witness JF-049, that the Defence was granted an extension of the deadline to respond until the 27th of April at 7.00 p.m., that is, yesterday. Meanwhile, the Prosecution has requested permission to reply and has replied, which under the present circumstances seems to be very practical although should be the exception rather than the rule, but under the present circumstances the Chamber does not oppose to this practice being applied under those circumstances. The reason being that the witness is in The Hague and that the Defence asked for a postponement of two months to start the testimony of this witness. We now know that the Prosecution disagrees with that. I don't think that we have received a response by the Stanisic -- Simatovic Defence. Did we receive a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. We joined Mr. Groome's motion, because that was the agreement, that Mr. Groome should make that motion, and we -- sorry, not Mr. Groome. Mr. Knoops, actually, and we joined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's a common position taken by the two Defence teams. Now, in the response, there was objection against admission of a new 92 ter statement. But there was another matter in the original motion which was that leave be granted to amend the 65 ter exhibit list by adding six exhibits attached. Is there any -- there was no response to adding those to the 65 ter list, as no issue was raised in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We don't take a point on that, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't take a point on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, adding documents to the 65 ter list is not yet admission, Mr. Groome, but in that respect, the request is granted. We'll -- I'll further discussion with the other Judges the request for a postponement of two months to start the examination-in-chief of Witness JF-049. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just an observation. The request for postponement was a secondary request. The primary request was to exclude the new statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I earlier said that there was an objection against admission of a new 92 ter statement, which was the primary relief sought, and subsidiarily that a delay of two months would be granted. One of the matters that I would like to inquire with the Defence: Is there anything in this new 92 ter statement which could not have been elicited viva voce from the witness to say that it was more or less in the context of the 65 ter summary of the witness, although giving -- that's for certain -- giving quite minimal details? Could that have been elicited from the witness as staying within the boundaries of the 65 ter -- 65 ter summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, an observation: On behalf of the Stanisic Defence, in addition to the motion filed, we observed that there was several new topics raised by the witness such as the paragraphs 40, 42, where he details the purported command structure of the JATD, which was not included in the summary. The same as the alleged command structure with Arkan units, paragraph 39, 46, of his supplementary statement. Paragraph 47 detailing also the position of Legija. And paragraph 65 where he goes into the alleged money stream of the JATD through allegedly offshore company. I think these are just examples of the many topics which were not included in the summary, and I think it's not obvious that these topics were to be elicited during the examination-in-chief, because that would go outside the boundaries of the -- the summary. And, by the way, it's also admission of Witness 049 himself, in paragraph 2 of his supplementary statement, where he indirectly admits that he's providing far more information than mentioned in his 2003 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He's giving far more -- certainly far more details. That especially names have been ... We'll consider the matter. Before we continue -- Yes, Mr. Groome. Would you like to stay anything in response to what Mr. Knoops just --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not on this point, Your Honour, but I do have another point that I would like to raise out of the witness's presence before he returns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I had on my mind to first -- Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to support everything that Mr. Knoops said. He mentioned paragraph 65, offshore companies and the funding of the JATD that is directly linked to my client, as well as paragraph 66, which contains a serious incrimination under our law, and all these are new allegations that were not included in the previous statement. We must verify that in detail and review it, but that is all along the lines of what Mr. Knoops had -- has already said and what can be found in the motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to ask Mr. Jordash how much time he would still need for cross-examination of the present witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If at all possible, I'd like another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which brings you -- yes, approximately at the upper end of your estimate, and that would be the end of today's session. Mr. Bakrac, who will -- how much -- or, Mr. Petrovic, how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to our current estimate, we will need up to three hours. We'll try hard to be briefer, but this is what we can say now. Of course, we have to hear what our learned friend Mr. Jordash will say until he finishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think we received information from Mr. Jordash, his original estimate. When did we -- did the Chamber receive your estimate, Mr. Petrovic? Did you send it by e-mail, or did you -- I think we invited you to give an estimate, to tell us how much time you would approximately need.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I stated that orally, Your Honours, and that I said two and a half hours then. I can check during the break and give you more reliable information, but I think at this moment that I gave you an oral statement to that effect toward the end of the previous session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just have a -- one second, please. What I see, Mr. Petrovic, is on last Friday's transcript that at the very end that I said: "The Defence is invited, if they have any further idea now having heard the examination-in-chief and knowing what will follow on Wednesday, to inform the Chamber about any assessment, any estimate, on the time they would need for cross-examination," and we then adjourned. So I don't remember that we have received any response to that invitation. Whether there has been an earlier assessment, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me, Your Honours, that it was earlier, but now I can't remember either. I believe I spoke about that, so with your leave I will check and try to find it during this break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we have -- of course, that was an estimate asked knowing, then, exactly what the examination-in-chief had -- had been. Now we have another perhaps little problem that for 92 ter witnesses the Chamber always has been -- well, I wouldn't use the word "generous," but at least not too strict in time because that's part of the 92 ter statement. Now, apparently the two Defence teams want for a witness who gave his testimony mainly viva voce, you would, nevertheless, almost ask -- coming close to the double of the time the Prosecution took, which is -- has there been any conversation between the two Defence teams on how to deal with this viva voce witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, hasn't -- well, there has been discussion, and we discussed which subjects we were going to cover, and I think we've tried to avoid duplication. Could I also, though, put this before the Chamber, that there is -- by agreeing -- by the Defence agreeing to having Milovanovic look at documents outside of the courtroom and thereby shorten the time the Prosecution took in the courtroom, we, in a sense, set ourselves up to have less time to cross-examine. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, this was not a matter of substance. This was -- I didn't hear any questions in cross-examination about the authenticity of documents, and that seems to be the only part of -- the only exercise that was requested from him out of court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution took the witness outside of court through a huge number of documents relating to the intelligence that Mr. Stanisic was receiving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I spent an hour dealing with that point as a consequence of the Prosecution putting in documents without discussing them in court with the point being powerfully, or at least on the face of it, powerfully made and having to be dealt with in cross-examination. That was the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time -- yes. Let's -- let's not -- we'll further think about the matter, and we'll have a break. And with the indulgence of Mr. Stanisic, I'd like to start at five minutes past 6.00 and then at least to see whether we could finish, if not earlier, and start the cross-examination by the Simatovic Defence, at least to finish today Mr. Jordash. We'll -- Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to be brief, but I think it is important that I raise this point with -- with the Chamber. It's in relation to 90(H). The Defence on several occasions has suggested to other witnesses that at least some of the crimes charged in the indictment against Mr. Stanisic and Simatovic were in fact prepared and perpetrated by members of the Army of the Republika Srpska. I would refer the Chamber to transcript 3799, line 20, as an example of such. It was taken in closed session, so I will not comment further now. Please also see the examination of JF-005 at transcript 2897 to 2901 or JF-10 at transcript 3799 to 3801. Given that the Chief of the Main Staff of that army is now here in court and is being questioned by the Defence and we are now to move into the last session of cross-examination by the Stanisic Defence, it is the Prosecution's position that 90(H)(ii) obliges the Defence to put to General Milovanovic those crimes described in the indictment which they allege was perpetrated by members of the Army of Republika Srpska and not through the participation of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic as alleged by the Prosecution, if that is, in fact, their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is about a witness contradicting the case of the examining party, isn't it, in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, to the extent the witness contradicts your case, you should put that case to the witness if you cross-examine him under Rule 90(H) and not just covering, not just challenging the evidence he has given on the questioning by the party that called him. Mr. Groome set out the rule. I can't say that at this moment I have a clear view on whether at this moment any obligation arises under Rule 90(H), although Mr. Groome thought at this moment that he should bring this to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My response to that would be twofold. Firstly, it would have been more practical if the Prosecution had given notice of this application. This is the first we've heard of it. And so I'm thinking off the top of my head. But my preliminary response to that would be that, as far as I understand it, the Rule 90(H) does not mandate that I have to put my case to any -- every witness who might somehow be able to say something about it. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not -- I think -- perhaps you take the break. It's my understanding of Rule (H) to say that if you examine a witness not challenging the examination by the party that called him but since the witness is able to give support to your case, that to the extent he contradicts your case, his evidence is contradicting your case, that you put at least clearly to the witness what your case is. But if it's contradicting your --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, of course, now the issue, whether the witness contradicted your case. Let's have, all, a look closer again at Rule 90(H). I didn't even read it again, but that's what my recollection tells me, Mr. Groome. And perhaps if you could briefly explain to Mr. Jordash during the break where you would expect him to do what exactly so that -- because he apparently is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll explain my point further, Your Honours, during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We will very a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one sentence. The Simatovic Defence apologises. We spoke with each other, and we were convinced that we also informed the Trial Chamber, but we didn't and I apologise. And it is our estimate that we will need the time just as I told you before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that observation, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say, as far as the obligations arises, we see them under 90(H), we shall put our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- you say you'll abide by the rules, and that's what we expect everyone to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have on e-court, please, 65 ter 577. This is slightly out of turn, because I will return to the previous topic, but I want to deal with this first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at this exhibit, Mr. Milovanovic. Is this document or the events it purports to describe familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. I don't remember ever having spoken to Tomislav Kovac about the arrest of deserters. I did speak to Arkan. I suppose that that's the commander of the Tigers. Yes. I can see now Zeljko Raznjatovic. However, we did not discuss this particular matter. As I already told you on Friday, we discussed the matter of him being chased away from the territory of the Republika Srpska by myself and General Mladic. I don't remember ever having spoken to anybody about the arrest of deserters. And the date here, as I can see, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the date here is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 11th of October, 1995, and a month before that Arkan was chased away from our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this then: Did you have -- let me strike that. Was there a problem with deserters from the front in the territory of the Prijedor CJB at this time or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a problem with the -- there was no problem with the deserters from the Republika Srpska Army. Those were final operations, and the combatants did not desert. But we did have problems with the combatants of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which practically disappeared in August 1995, and nobody organised the withdrawal of those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got 35 minutes left, so I'm going to have to cut you off, and I do apologise for being rude.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I apply to tender this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D40, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon. It's already an exhibit, D28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D28, if it's that already, then we vacate D40. Is it with the same translation, because it seems that the name of this witness, which in the original is Milovanovic, seems to be abbreviated to Milanovic in my translation on my screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I check that and inform the Court later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to return quickly and move quickly, Mr. Milovanovic, to the subject we were dealing with before. You talked about a meeting which involved Stanisic, Badza, Panic, and Mladic at the Hotel Omorika on the 23rd of January, 1993. Can you confirm that Stanisic and Badza had arrived from Bajina Basta and from Bajina Basta had come to Tara? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, General Mladic was not in attendance at that meeting. He was in Geneva. Secondly, I don't know how come Mr. Stanisic was at Tara in Omorika Hotel. I don't know whether he arrived with Panic by helicopter or in another way, and I really don't know where he came from. I don't have a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that Sokolovic, the minister, had been present earlier with Stanisic and Badza in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I actually saw Sokolovic only once at a meeting in December, on the 13 of December, 1993, in Belgrade, and that's the only time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. When you heard Badza make the comment, "I arrived here with my boss," Stanisic was sitting very close to him, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four of us at -- sitting at a small table. I believe that we were in the lobby of the Omorika Hotel, and since there were four of us, two of us had to sit next to each other. I don't know where Badza was sitting in relation to Mr. Panisic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: They were within feet of each other, weren't they? "Yes" or "No" will do, I think.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when Badza said, "I arrived here with my boss," in no way did he gesture towards Stanisic, did he? Which you might have expected, I would suggest, if he was referring to Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was asked the same thing on Friday. After 17 years, it's very difficult to remember people's gestures or facial expressions. As far as I can remember, he did not point in Stanisic's direction, but I really don't know whether that is relevant at this moment, whether he pointed at him or not. He said, "I arrived with my boss," and that was enough for me. I didn't even know who his boss was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that Badza at that point was the deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia, a position, we suggest, which was higher than Mr. Stanisic's?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time. I only learnt that subsequently, much later, that Badza was the deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia. On that very day, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, just to be clear, you learnt that he was the deputy minister of the interior in January 1993, and you learnt that information later; is that what you're saying? I want to establish when it was that you -- I mean -- let me rephrase that. How long after did you find out that Badza was the deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when. Perhaps even on that very evening when I arrived at the Main Staff, when I described Jovica Stanisic for them I didn't know who he was. Let me not repeat how I described Jovica Stanisic. And then either Tolimir or Beara told me, "Well, that was Jovica Stanisic, the head of the state security of Serbia." And then when I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the witness be allowed to finish that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then on that very evening I learned that Badza was in charge of special units of the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the special units of the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior fell under the public security, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, we had two Special Police brigades, and they were under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior, but not as bodies of public security. But I don't even know what Special Police Units are used for. I know what we use them for in war time, but in peacetime I don't know what their purpose is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. I don't wish to ask you about that. But I do want to ask you about one thing, and I don't want to embarrass anyone, but you thought at that meeting on the 23rd of January, 1993, that Stanisic was a waiter, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I beg Stanisic's pardon, but that's what I thought. He was well dressed, he was very polite, he was well mannered, he was well-groomed. I thought he was a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now move on. Could you explain, if you can remember, what Operation Udar was that we talked about last week?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Udar was an operation undertaken by our army which concerned the battle against Naser Oric and placing under the Serb control of the area that I showed on the map earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm that Jovica Stanisic had no role in that operation other than to provide intelligence assessments?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Jovica Stanisic during that operation. I don't even remember that I heard anything about him or in relation to him during that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I mean, it's a long time ago, but your best recollection is that his name didn't come up during the discussions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move on to the last subject I think I'm going to deal with, which is operation -- actually, it's the second to last subject, Operation Pauk. Are you able to just give the Trial Chamber a short, short summary on the background, as you understood it, to Operation Pauk, the military and humanitarian background to Operation Pauk? Start with the military, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about the humanitarian part of that because I don't know. As far as the military part is concerned, I know that that was a joint operation by the Serbian Army of Krajina -- or, rather, the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the forces under the command of Fikret Abdic. They joined forces in order to liquidate or to defeat the 5th Corps of the so-called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I know that the person in command was General Mile Novakovic, who had previously been removed from the position as commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Serbian Krajina. He was too young to be pensioned off; therefore, he was appointed the advisor for national security to President Martic. When the Operation Pauk was launched, and it was launched around the time when I launched a counter-attack in the direction of Bihac with the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska, that was in November, that was the time when I first heard about the future operation. It was a future operation at the time, on the 8th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Let's just deal with what was happening before the future operation, before Operation Pauk. Was there an involvement of the VRS in the Muslim conflict?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you've just spoken about a future operation, but you talked about a counter-attack in the direction of Bihac before that future operation. Could you explain the counter-operation -- the counter-attack? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Shall I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Here we go. On the 19th, the 20th, and the 21st of August, 1994, the 5th Corps of the so-called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina defeated the forces of the -- of national defence of the Autonomous Province of West Bosnia, i.e., Fikret Abdic. Abdic had about 10- to 12.000 combatants who were all defeated. That was an internal inter-Muslim conflict. It was not an ethnic or a religious conflict. It was an internal conflict or typical civil war. And after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just pause you there. As a consequence of Fikret Abdic's army being defeated, what happened -- were there any refugees?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and as far as I read in the intelligence, some 72.000 people who were supporters of Fikret Abdic were exiled from that area and enclosed in two camps, one in Batnoge in the Bihac region, and the other one was somewhere in the north in the territory of Croatia, either south of Cicak or south of Karlovac. I'm not sure. Fikret's autonomous province thus ceased to exist. The new commander of the 5th Corps, Atif Dudakovic, was encouraged by that success, and he launched an attack against Republika Srpska in the territory stretching from Krupa on the River Una upstream to Bihac and from Bihac again upstream to Kula and Vakuf. Over the seven days of combat, from the 23rd of October to the 30th of October, he managed to occupy some 250 square kilometres of the territory of Republika Srpska. In practical terms, he occupied Mount Grmec and all the villages at the foot of Mount Grmec.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. Could I stop you there a moment. Is it correct that Alija Izetbegovic quenched Fikret Abdic's rebellion and as a consequence imprisoned 70.000 Muslims in two camps? These were 70.000 civilians in the main in two camps.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you asking me? You're asking me if something is correct? You mentioned Alija Izetbegovic. You mentioned the camps. Are you asking me whether it is true that Alija Izetbegovic issued that order or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether Alija Izetbegovic imprisoned 70.000 civilians in two camps, having defeated Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't Alija Izetbegovic who did that. It was General Atif Dudakovic who did that. And it was Alija Izetbegovic who issued an order to him to quench the rebellion in blood because he considered Fikret Abdic a rebel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The man you've just mentioned, Atif Dudakovic, was the commander of the 5th Corps acting under Izetbegovic's direction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you yourself were sufficiently concerned about the 5th Corps's treatment of civilians that you suggested to Mladic that you should file charges against him for crimes against civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, can I just ask you to return to your narrative. I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let me finish that first. That proposal was turned down with an explanation along the lines, We should not get involved in their business, in their showdown. But the real reason was the fact that the Republika Srpska had not recognised The Hague Tribunal at the moment when it was set up pursuant to Resolution 817. So if we were to sue Dudakovic for war crimes, that would have implied that we recognised the Tribunal. And now let me go back to the narrative. When Dudakovic did what he did --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just remember what you're saying is being translated, so just remember to pause. Go ahead. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] When Atif Dudakovic and his corps did what they did, what ensued was a breakdown in our 2nd Krajina Corps. That corps, from the moment of its establishment up to then, had not been involved in any major combat. What they were involved in was, rather, a trench war which lasted for two and a half years up to then. And that corps was simply entrenched on the right bank of the Una and waited there. I suppose that by that time both the command cadre and the troops had become very relaxed, and that's how Dudakovic managed to do what he did in the space of only seven days. The Supreme Command of Republika Srpska appointed me and ordered me to go to Mount Grmec and see what was going on there. Since we all knew what was going on, I asked from the supreme commander to allow me to do something, since they were sending me there. The implication was that I should try and return the lost territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. What -- had the 5th Corps taken 250 square kilometres of Serbian territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 5th Muslim Corps of the so-called Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina commanded by Atif Dudakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. Sorry to interrupt again.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My requests to the supreme commander were about the following: First, until the time when I get to Grmec, declare the state of war at least in that area for me to be able to deal with the deserters from the 2nd Krajina Corps. Before that, the corps was about 14.500 strong. And I only found some 6500 organised combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did the --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done when I arrived at Grmec. The state of war was in effect in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. I employed the military school centre as an operational reserve of the Main Staff and introduced them into combat on the 30th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was the objective of the combat from the perspective of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the objective of the counter-strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective was to take the lost territory again, to take possession of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The military objective; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military objective or the objective of the operation. Later, I termed it "Stit 94," Shield 94.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about Suckin [phoen]? Was it a successful military operation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was successful. We were able to return the lost territory within 57 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at what point in time was that? When did it succeed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I launched the counter-strike on the 3rd of November, and it was completed in 57 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: November of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what happened after that? Was there a further operation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, as far as the VRS is concerned, with the assistance of Jimmy Carter, the former US president, a four-month truce began between us and the so-called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we -- both sides started going about our own business on -- in our respective territories. But we don't seem to be getting to Operation Pauk. I started, but you interrupted me. On the 8th of November, 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was invited by Milan Martic, the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and I must say that he cheated me. He asked me to come to Bosanski Petrovac so that he could talk to me, and I said that it was difficult for me to get there in a vehicle because I would have to come over Mount Grmec and that would be a long detour. And I couldn't fly there by helicopter because there was a flight ban pursuant to Resolution 816 of the UN Security Council. He said, I'll send you a white helicopter. Which was probably given to him by UNPROFOR to use. I agreed, but as the helicopter was a different model than the ones that we were using, so I took a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could I cut you short. Martic tricked you into attending, is that right, attending a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He tricked me because the pilot didn't take me to Petrovac. He took me to Plitvice instead -- or, to be more precise, to the Slunj range where there was some kind of forward command post of his supreme command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Forward command post for what?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please, I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Witness, and I would really like if you could explain to the Chamber what Operation Pauk was designed to do. What was the military objectives behind Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of Operation Pauk, as I understood it to be on that 8th of November, was that Fikret Abdic should have his comeback in the Bihac region. The second objective was the destruction of the 5th Corps so that Fikret Abdic could establish control over the entire Cazin area, the Cazin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was part of that objective to allow refugees who'd - excuse me - who'd gathered in the Kordun region to return home to the Bihac region?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The refugees had already been returned pursuant to a decision of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Operation Pauk successful?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but you're not letting me say what I want to in order to avoid these follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, you've got seven minutes. I'd been happy if you'd explain as much relevant detail as you can of the military Operation Pauk, please. I'll try not to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Well, in that room, I found 11 officers with their boss, Fikret Abdic. There was also the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Mr. Martic, and of the other people I knew, I also saw the commander of the Serbian Army of the Krajina, General Celeketic. I saw Jovica Stanisic, but he meant nothing to me then. I don't know what they had been discussing before. When I entered the room, I don't even remember welcoming or saying hello to anyone. I immediately spoke to Martic, criticising me why he had tricked me. The commander of the Serb army, Mr. Celeketic, then explained to me why I had been brought there. The Serb army of the Krajina wanted to resuscitate Fikret Abdic's army, and for that purpose I was supposed to give them 6.000 barrels, and Celeketic would give them 5.000, and that I was supposed to launch an offensive toward Bihac with my forces. I replied that I was not authorised by my Supreme Command or the commander of the Main Staff to negotiate with Martic's command at all, and especially not with Fikret Abdic. I didn't even say hello to Fikret Abdic on that occasion. I said that I wouldn't give them any weapons, because I had said as much to Karadzic on the 23rd of October, 1993, the day after he had signed the agreement on permanent peace with Fikret Abdic. And he wanted the army to give weapons to Fikret Abdic, and I said okay, but only what the government of the RS had provided to the RS, which means, in other words, nothing. As for my offensive toward Bihac, I said that it was in progress and that I had come about halfway, as far as the Una. Spasovo had already been taken; the old name of that place was Kulen Vakuf. We were able to defend Krupa on the Una, so it was possible for me to advance towards Bihac from Krupa and turn Kulen Vakuf into tongs, which is the dream of any general. That was the strategy. But I couldn't promise them any other co-ordinated action because I had no authority. I asked Martic to give orders for the helicopter to take me back, and that's what happened. After that, Operation Pauk followed. I know that the Serbs from the Republic of Serbian Krajina were advancing along the axis of Trzaska Rastela-Cazin. That was a long axis. And Fikret Abdic had received the assignment to re-establish his lost authority, his government. And the activities continued in the following year, and I believe it went on until the end of the war. The 5th Corps was not defeated. Fikret Abdic fell through once again, and those were the -- that was the outcome of Operation Pauk.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. From what you've said, can you confirm that this operation had nothing to do with forcible transfer of civilians? Its objectives were purely military, regaining territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was no violence against civilians. Only Dudakovic misused the civilians. He brought population from the surrounding villages into Bihac, but he did that while I was attacking him. So there were 100.000 -- 180.000 people in Bihac. I don't know how large it was before the war. He turned Bihac into a military target because that's where his forces were resting, but he was actually using civilians as a human shield because we couldn't shell Bihac because of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you didn't shell Bihac because of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS has never shelled Bihac. That was an order that we received from the Supreme Command, that we mustn't use larger calibre weapons than 12.7 millimetres to target Bihac. And in every order of mine, there is the sentence, "I forbid the use of larger calibre weapons than 12.7 millimetres to attack Bihac."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I ask two more questions, Your Honour, then I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not my time, primarily, that you're stealing, but from all those who are assisting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll be extremely quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'll be blamed for it. Two short questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you met Stanisic, Jovica Stanisic, he meant nothing to you, and you didn't know what role he was playing in the Pauk operation. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between my first encounter with Jovica Stanisic and the launch of Operation Pauk, much time elapsed, almost three years. So I hope that Mr. Stanisic will not mind me saying that during that period he meant nothing at all to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you met him, when you were being requested to be the commander of Pauk, you didn't know what role, if any, he was playing in Pauk; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he had any role at all in that operation. I thought he had been sent from Belgrade to tell me what he told me. We spoke about that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Before we adjourn, I already instruct you, Mr. Milovanovic, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony or communicate in any other way about testimony already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Madam Usher will now escort you out of the courtroom so that I have one more second to deal with another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I get some approximate information as to the duration of my stay here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will try to finish your testimony tomorrow. That's what, really, we want to do. Now, as far as travelling back, whether a flight can be found for you in time, that may cause a problem. As you are aware, European air traffic is quite a bit disturbed and we are still suffering. So we try to finish your testimony tomorrow, and I'll urge the parties that it should be done. But I'm not in charge of the travel arrangements. What I do know is that the Victims and Witnesses Section always try to get people home again as soon as they can, but I can't give you any guarantees at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to make a few observations in relation to the next witness. Comparing the new 92 ter statements with the old ones and with the 65 ter summary, we find that sometimes it's just explaining, giving further details, but very much more of the same. Sometimes, however, matters appear to be quite new. Mr. Groome, correct me when I'm wrong. I had not prepared for that witness for today, but, for example, the financing from Cyprus restaurants is not something that rang a bell to me. That's -- paragraph 65 seems to be entirely knew to me or -- is that correct, or have I overlooked something?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, you haven't, Your Honour. That's something -- mentioned to the witness. The Prosecution will not rely on it and may not even ask about, Your Honour, if the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the Defence has to prepare for it if you want it to be in evidence, isn't it? Well, some areas also seem to be very easy to verify, sometimes could even be in the direct knowledge of the accused so that they could instruct counsel; whereas for other areas it might be -- well, quite burdensome to explore. Sometimes it's also a mixture. If we're talking about licence plates, it could well be that I have some knowledge about licence plates in my environment, but, of course, you may want to verify that in further detail. So sometimes it is a mixture of easy and perhaps cumbersome. Sometimes the information given is quite trivial, whereas other information seems to have a higher level of -- of relevance. Now, the Chamber has not made up its mind yet, but, for example, if you say, "I'm not going to rely on the Cyprus restaurants," why not then redact it? So for the -- for the Defence to know that they don't have to pay attention to it and have not to further explore the names of those restaurants, whether they were owned, whether the money came from there, whether the sources - it's all hearsay - whether they're reliable or not. So that's one option. Another option would be to gain a bit of additional time, and let's say to start on a Wednesday rather than on Monday. That's an option which gives at least some additional time to -- to prepare. Of course, there's another option for the Prosecution to postpone, but that requires then that you'd have witnesses available either on Monday or on Wednesday. We're trying to consider all this. It seems as the Prosecution may oversimplify matters at this moment, whereas the Defence here may overdramatise matters. The Chamber at this moment certainly is not at a point that they would decide not to admit. The Chamber is certainly not granting two more months to prepare, and we'll think it over, perhaps further discuss it tomorrow, and invite, meanwhile, the parties, whether by redacting, by agreeing on what's really very relevant and what is rather trivial -- I mean, if we are talking dramatically about - what was is? - 28 pages -- well, part of those 28 pages are taken by -- I recognise this as a per diem list, et cetera. That's, of course, not as dramatic new information that the witness recognises these as per diem lists and then says, "I see these in these names which --" so, therefore, I would urge the parties to see whether they could come to any conclusion. Of course, otherwise the Chamber will decide. You know what is on our mind at this moment. You also know that there seems to be a tendency of overdramatising and oversimplifying. If you get that out of the way, if you would come with a solution which would fit the parties, the Chamber will seriously consider to follow that. The approaches adopted until now have not yet convinced the Chamber that we could either choose the first, the primary option, or the second one. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I also ask the Court to consider that - Mr. Weber was scheduled to do this -- to lead this evidence and finds himself in somewhat unusual personal circumstances - that the Chamber also consider the option of allowing the Prosecution to lead as much evidence as possible and then with a view towards, if the Chamber wishes, to grant some time for cross -- additional time to prepare for cross-examination for new information that we simply bifurcate the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that, but let's put matters simple. Some matters are better to be foreseen well in advance, as others are. Now, to in any way jeopardise the position of the Defence where perhaps for quite a number of months the personal circumstances of Mr. Weber could have been foreseen is not something which is first on our mind. Yes? We adjourn. I thank all those who have, again, assisted us. And we'll resume tomorrow, the 29th of April, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of April, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.10 p.m.,
